title: How heat moves: why a steel spoon in hot tea gets hot

summary.text: Leave a steel spoon standing in hot tea, and in a minute or two its handle is warm, though only the bottom touched the tea. Heat has travelled up through the solid steel. Heat always moves from a hotter thing to a cooler one, and through a solid it passes from each tiny part to the part next to it. This is called conduction. In this unit your child puts butter dots along a steel ladle in hot water and times them as they melt, one after another. They find that heat reaches the near dots fast, the far dots slowly, and the farthest dot perhaps never.
summary.art: A steel ladle standing in a tumbler of steaming water, with four small butter dots along the handle, the lowest one melting and a peppercorn sliding off it.

intro.hook: Stand a steel spoon in a cup of hot tea for two minutes. Touch the top of the handle. It is warm, though it never touched the tea. How did the heat get up there?
intro.text: No hot tea climbed up the spoon. Only the bottom of the spoon is in the tea. Yet the handle warms, slowly, from the bottom up. In this unit you find out how heat travels through a solid, and how fast. You time butter melting along a ladle, you hold ice in your fist, and you find out why a dosa tawa has a wooden handle.
intro.art: A cup of tea on a kitchen counter with a steel spoon standing in it, and a child's finger gently touching the tip of the spoon handle while a grown-up watches.

outcomes: By the end I can say which way heat moves: from a hotter thing to a cooler one.
By the end I can explain how heat travels through a solid spoon, part by part, and call it conduction.
By the end I can show, from my ladle test, that heat reaches near parts first and far parts later, and some heat escapes into the air on the way.
By the end I can name materials that carry heat fast (metals) and slowly (wood, plastic, cloth, air), and say why pans have metal bottoms and wooden or plastic handles.
By the end I can plan a fair test, guess with a reason, and say what I think, what I saw and why.
By the end I can explain that cold does not move into my hand: heat moves out of it.

terms.meaning: Energy that moves from a hotter thing to a cooler thing.
terms.example: Heat moves from hot tea into the steel spoon standing in it.

terms.meaning: How hot or cold something is. We measure it in degrees Celsius, written °C.
terms.example: Hot tea is about 60 °C. A room in Chennai in summer can be about 32 °C.

terms.meaning: Heat moving through a material, or from one thing into another thing it touches, part by part, with nothing flowing.

terms.meaning: A material that lets heat move through it quickly. Metals are good conductors of heat.

explanations.context: This card says which way heat always goes.
explanations.concept: Heat moves from hotter to cooler
explanations.definition: Heat moves by itself from a hotter thing to a cooler thing. It keeps moving until both are equally warm.
explanations.description: Hot tea warms the spoon in it. The spoon never cools the tea down to colder than the room. An ice cube in your hand melts because heat moves from your hand into the ice. Your hand feels cold because it is losing heat. No cold comes out of the ice. Heat never moves by itself from a cooler thing to a hotter one. A fridge can make that happen only because it uses electricity to pump the heat out.
examples: Hot rasam in a steel bowl warms the bowl, and the bowl warms the table under it.
A cold bottle from the fridge gets warmer on the table, because heat moves into it from the warmer room.
explanations.art: A hot cup and an ice cube side by side, each with a red arrow: from the cup into the air, and from the air into the ice.

explanations.context: This card explains how heat travels through a solid spoon, which does not flow or move.
explanations.concept: Conduction: heat passed from part to part
explanations.definition: Conduction is heat moving through a material, from each tiny part to the part touching it.
explanations.description: The particles in a solid are packed tightly and are always shaking a little. The hotter a thing is, the faster its particles shake. Hot tea makes the particles at the bottom of the spoon shake faster. They knock into the particles just above them, and those start to shake faster too. Those knock into the next ones, and so on up the handle. No particle travels up the spoon. Each one stays in its place and passes the shaking on. That passed-on shaking is the heat you feel in the handle.
examples: The steel handle of a ladle in hot sambar warms from the bottom up.
Your hand warms a cold steel tumbler where your fingers touch it, then the warmth spreads around the tumbler.
explanations.art: A row of tiny balls inside a spoon handle: at the hot end they shake hard with motion lines, and each ball nudges the next, the shaking getting smaller further up.

explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the Ladle Line test: why the far butter dots melted so much later.
explanations.concept: Why heat reaches far parts late, or not at all
explanations.definition: Heat travelling through a solid reaches nearby parts quickly and far parts much more slowly. Some of it escapes into the air along the way.
explanations.description: Before heat can move past a part of the spoon, it must first warm that part. So each part has to wait for the part before it. That is why the waits grow longer as you go further along. Twice as far takes much more than twice as long. All the way along, the warm steel also gives some heat to the air around it. So less heat is left for the far end. On a long ladle, the far end may never get hot at all. That is one reason ladles for hot sambar have long handles.
examples: On the Ladle Line, the dot 2 cm up may melt in under a minute, while the dot 8 cm up may never melt.
The end of a long iron skewer held in a fire stays cool enough to hold for a while, while the tip glows.
explanations.art: A ladle handle drawn as a long strip, coloured red at the bottom fading through orange to yellow and then grey at the top, with small wavy lines leaving the sides into the air.

explanations.context: This card is about why some materials carry heat fast and others slowly.
explanations.definition: A conductor of heat lets heat through quickly. An insulator of heat lets it through only very slowly.
explanations.description: Metals are good conductors of heat. Wood, plastic, cloth, paper and still air are insulators. Metals are not all the same, though. Copper and aluminium carry heat many times faster than the stainless steel most Indian spoons are made of. That is why some steel vessels have a copper or aluminium layer on the bottom. Cooks use both kinds of material together. The pan is metal, so heat reaches the food fast. The handle is wood or plastic, so heat reaches your hand slowly.
examples: A dosa tawa: an iron or aluminium plate with a wooden handle.
A pressure cooker: an aluminium or steel pot with plastic handles.
A coconut-shell ladle, used in many Kerala kitchens, stays cool to hold in hot curry.
explanations.art: A kitchen shelf with a tawa, a pressure cooker and a coconut-shell ladle, each with its metal part coloured red and its handle coloured blue.

explanations.context: This card explains why metals carry heat so well, from inside the atom.
explanations.concept: Why metals are such good conductors
explanations.definition: In a metal, some tiny particles called electrons are free to move about between the atoms. They carry heat quickly from the hot part to the cool part.
explanations.description: Every atom has electrons on its outside. In wood or plastic, the electrons stay tied to their own atoms. Then heat can only be passed on by atoms nudging their neighbours, which is slow. In a metal, some electrons wander freely through the whole piece. They pick up energy in the hot part and quickly carry it to the cool part. These free electrons are also why metals carry electricity. So the best conductors of electricity, like silver and copper, are also the best conductors of heat.
examples: Copper carries both heat and electricity very well. It is used in electric wires and in the bottoms of good cooking pots.
Wood carries neither heat nor electricity well.
explanations.art: Inside a metal: big atoms in neat rows, with small bright dots, the electrons, zipping between them from a red hot end to a blue cool end.

explanations.context: This card shows two other ways heat moves, which you will learn more about in Class 5.
explanations.definition: Heat can also be carried by a moving liquid or gas, and it can travel as invisible rays.
explanations.description: In a pan of water on the stove, the hot water at the bottom rises and cooler water sinks to take its place. This is called convection. It is why the whole pan heats, though only the bottom touches the flame. The Sun's heat reaches us across empty space, where there is nothing to pass it on. It comes as rays we cannot see. This is called radiation. You feel it on your face near a fire, without touching anything. A spoon in tea gets hot mainly by conduction.
examples: Steam and hot air rising above a pot of boiling rice is convection.
Your face feeling warm in the sun is radiation.
explanations.art: Three small pictures in a row: a spoon in tea (conduction), a pan of water with curling arrows going up and down (convection), and the Sun shining on a child's face (radiation).

agreed.text: Heat moves by itself only from hotter things to cooler things.
agreed.evidence: Every test ever done agrees: hot things cool to the temperature around them, and cold things warm up to it. No one has ever seen heat move by itself the other way.

agreed.text: In a solid, heat travels by conduction, passed from part to part.
agreed.evidence: Butter or wax on a metal rod melts in order, starting nearest the heat, as Jan Ingenhousz saw on his wax-coated wires in 1780.

agreed.text: Metals are good conductors of heat, and wood, plastic, cloth and still air are insulators.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have measured how fast heat moves through thousands of materials. Copper carries heat more than a thousand times faster than wood.

agreed.text: The hotter a thing is, the faster its particles move.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can measure the speed of particles in gases, and it rises as the gas gets hotter. A drop of food colour also spreads faster in hot water than in cold, because the water particles are moving faster.

challenging.context: Does heat always go up? This card looks at a common saying.
challenging.for: Hot air and hot water do rise, and steam goes up from a pot. The top of a room is often warmer than the floor.
challenging.against: It is hot air and hot water that rise, because they are lighter than the cool air or water around them. Inside a solid, heat goes every way. A spoon lying flat with its bowl in hot water warms along its handle just as an upright one does. Heat goes from hotter to cooler, in whatever direction that is.

challenging.context: Does cold go into your hand when you hold ice? This card looks at that idea.
challenging.claim: When you hold ice, cold moves from the ice into your hand.
challenging.who: A very common way of talking
challenging.for: Your hand feels cold, and it really does get colder.
challenging.against: Your hand gets colder because heat moves out of it into the ice. That is why the ice melts. Cold is not a thing that moves. It is only less heat.

challenging.context: Are all metals alike? This card looks at a common guess.
challenging.claim: All metals carry heat equally well.
challenging.who: An easy guess, because metals look and feel alike
challenging.for: All metals are conductors of heat, and all feel cold to touch.
challenging.against: When Jan Ingenhousz tested wax-coated wires in 1780, the wax melted farthest on silver and least far on lead. Today we know copper carries heat about 25 times faster than stainless steel.

big_questions.q: No particle of the spoon travelled up to the handle. So what exactly moved up the spoon?
big_questions.hint: Think of a line of people passing on a push, each one staying in their place.

big_questions.q: The far end of your ladle stayed cool. Where did the heat go that never reached it?
big_questions.hint: Hold your hand near the middle of a warm ladle, without touching it.

big_questions.q: Your body is warmer than the room almost all the time. So heat is leaving you all day. Where does your body get more?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you ate today.

big_questions.q: Heat always spreads out from hot places to cool ones. If that goes on for ever, will everything in the universe one day be the same temperature?
big_questions.hint: Scientists have asked this too. Some think so, but nobody knows for sure.

big_questions.q: Why would a cook want one part of a vessel to be a good conductor and another part to be a good insulator?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the heat should go, and where it should not.

story.title: The Ladle in the Payasam
story.note: The story is made up. The science in it is true: heat moves up a steel ladle by conduction, near parts first, and wood and coconut shell are insulators of heat.
text: It was the morning of Onam, and Meenu's flat in Kochi smelled of ghee and jaggery. Meenu was eight. Her cousin Arjun was six, and he had come from Thrissur for the festival. In the kitchen, Meenu's ammayi, Revathi, was stirring a big pot of payasam on the gas stove.
"Meenu, will you stir for a minute?" said Ammayi. "I must fetch the cashews."
Meenu loved stirring payasam. She took hold of the long steel ladle where Ammayi had left it standing in the pot. Then she let go at once.
"Ow! It's hot!" She shook her fingers.
Arjun peered at the ladle. "But you only touched the top. The top isn't in the payasam."
"I know," said Meenu, frowning. "It was hot anyway."
Ammayi came back with the cashews. She took a folded cloth and lifted the ladle out. "Show me your fingers," she said. They were pink, but fine. Ammayi ran them under the cold tap for a while.
"How did the top get hot?" asked Meenu. "The payasam didn't climb up the ladle."
"No, it didn't," said Ammayi. "Let's find out. You two can do an experiment while the payasam cools."

She gave Meenu a clean steel ladle and a little butter from the fridge. Meenu put four small dots of butter along the handle, a finger-width apart. Arjun pressed a peppercorn into each dot. Ammayi poured hot water from the kettle into a steel tumbler and stood the ladle in it, with the dots facing up.
"Which peppercorn will fall first?" asked Ammayi.
"The top one," said Arjun at once. "Because heat goes up."
"The bottom one," said Meenu. "Because it is nearest the hot water."
They watched. For a little while nothing happened. Then the lowest dot went shiny, and its peppercorn slid down into the tumbler with a tiny plop.
"Mine!" said Meenu.
A long time later, the second peppercorn slid off. Then they waited, and waited, for the third. Arjun counted to a hundred twice before it moved. The top peppercorn did not fall at all.
"The heat is slow," said Arjun. "It got tired."

Ammayi laughed. "Heat doesn't get tired. But you've seen something real. Imagine the ladle is made of tiny pieces, far too small to see, all in a line. The hot water makes the bottom pieces shake faster. They bump the pieces above them, and those start shaking too. The heat is passed up, piece by piece. Each piece has to warm up before it can pass the heat on. So the far pieces have to wait a long time."
"Why didn't the top one ever melt?" asked Meenu.
"Hold your hand near the middle of the ladle," said Ammayi. "Don't touch it."
Meenu held her palm close to the handle. "It's a bit warm, even in the air."

"Yes. The ladle gives some of its heat to the air all along the way," said Ammayi. "By the time it gets near the top, not much is left. This is called conduction. It's how heat moves through a solid."
Arjun looked at the ladle, then at the stove. "Then why doesn't the dosa tawa burn your hand when you hold it?"
"Go and look at its handle," said Ammayi.
Arjun fetched the tawa from the shelf. Its handle was made of wood. "Wood!" he said.

"Wood is an insulator of heat," said Ammayi. "Heat moves through it very slowly. Metal is a good conductor. That's why the pan is metal and the handle is wood. The heat goes into the dosa, not into my hand."

Meenu thought for a moment. Then she opened the bottom drawer and pulled out something brown and round on a stick. It was Ammamma's old chiratta ladle, a ladle made from half a coconut shell with a wooden handle.
"Can we stir the payasam with this one?" she asked.
"That's what Ammamma always did," said Ammayi, smiling. "Try it."
Meenu stirred the payasam slowly, round and round. The handle stayed cool in her hand all the way through. Arjun watched the steam curling up from the pot.
"Ammayi," he said, "the steam goes up. So does heat go up, or not?"

"Hot steam rises, because it is lighter than the air," said Ammayi. "But in the ladle, heat goes from hot to cool, whichever way that is. Up, down or sideways. Tomorrow you can test it with a ladle lying flat."
That afternoon, the whole family ate payasam on banana leaves. Arjun said it was the best payasam in Kerala, because it had been stirred with a cool spoon.
story.epiphany: Heat moves through a solid ladle part by part, from the hot end towards the cool end. It reaches near parts first and far parts much later, and wood and coconut shell let it through so slowly that a handle made of them stays cool.
ask: Why did the top of the steel ladle burn Meenu's fingers, when it was not in the payasam?
Arjun guessed the top peppercorn would fall first, because heat goes up. What did the test show?
Why do you think the top peppercorn never fell?
Why does a tawa have a wooden handle?

games.title: Pass the Heat: a board game along a ladle
games.context: This is a board game. Each player is a bit of heat, travelling from the hot sambar up the ladle handle to the cook's hand. Metal squares speed you up, and air and wood slow you down.

printables.title: The ladle board
items: A long ladle drawn across the page, with 20 squares along its handle. Square 1 is in the hot sambar and square 20 is the cook's hand.
Squares 5 and 12 say 'Leak into the air: go back 2'.
Squares 8 and 16 say 'Wooden grip: miss a turn'.

printables.title: 24 move cards to cut out
items: 3 AIR cards: move back 1, because heat leaks into the air

printables.title: 12 question cards
items: Which way does heat move by itself? (From hotter to cooler)
What is heat moving through a solid called? (Conduction)
Name a good conductor of heat. (Any metal, such as steel, copper or aluminium)
Name an insulator of heat. (Wood, plastic, cloth, paper or still air)
Why does a tawa have a wooden handle? (Wood lets heat through slowly, so your hand stays cool)
On the Ladle Line, which dot melts first? (The one nearest the hot water)
Does heat inside a spoon only go up? (No. It moves from hot to cool, any way)
You hold ice. Does cold go into your hand? (No. Heat goes out of your hand)
Which carries heat faster, copper or steel? (Copper)
Who tested wax-coated wires in 1780? (Jan Ingenhousz)
Why did the top dot on the ladle not melt? (The heat had far to go, and some leaked into the air)
What shakes faster: particles in hot steel or cold steel? (Hot steel)

printables.title: Tokens
items: One red bead, button or coin for each player

rules: Put every player's token on square 1, in the sambar. Shuffle the move cards and put them face down. Put the question cards face down too.
On your turn, take a move card and move your token. Then follow what the square says.
Instead of a move card, you may answer a question card. Answer right, and move on 2. Answer wrong, and stay where you are.
The first player to reach square 20, the cook's hand, wins. Playing alone, try to reach the hand in 12 turns.
When you win, say one way the cook could have kept you away from her hand.

flow.do: 1. Print or draw the board and cards. 2. Put the tokens on square 1. 3. Read the rules together.
flow.say: You are a bit of heat in the hot sambar. You want to get to the cook's hand. Metal helps you. Wood and air slow you down.
flow.kid: You are heat in the sambar. Get to the cook's hand first.

flow.do: Play the game. When someone lands on an AIR or WOOD square, ask why it slows the heat.
flow.say: Why does a wood card not move you at all?
flow.kid: Play. When you get a wood card, say why it stops you.

ask.q: Why does a wood card not move you?
good: Heat moves through wood very slowly.

flow.do: When the game ends, ask the winner to say how the cook could stop the heat.
flow.say: How could the cook keep the heat away from her hand?
flow.kid: How could the cook keep heat away from her hand?

check.q: Which handle would keep a cook's hand coolest on a hot pan?
check.why: Wood is an insulator of heat, so heat moves through it very slowly. Steel and copper are metals, good conductors. Copper is the fastest of the three, so it would get hot quickest.

experiments.title: The Ladle Line: how does heat climb a steel ladle?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put butter dots along a steel ladle, stand it in hot water, and time each dot as it melts. It shows how heat travels through a solid, and how fast.
experiments.question: When a steel ladle stands in hot water, do all the butter dots on its handle melt at once, or one after another? And does the farthest one melt at all?
experiments.predict: Look at the four butter dots on the handle. Which will melt first, and which last? Will they melt close together or far apart in time? Will the top one melt at all? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every butter dot is the same size, about half a pea, with one peppercorn in it. The dots are 2, 4, 6 and 8 cm above the water. Only the distance changes. One more dot sits on a spoon on a plate, out of the water, to show what the room alone does to butter.

materials.item: a long steel ladle, such as a sambar or rasam karandi, at least 20 cm long. A long steel serving spoon also works.
a steel spoon, for the room-butter dot
a steel tumbler or mug that the ladle can lean in without tipping
hot water from a kettle or a pan, just off the boil, poured by a grown-up
butter straight from the fridge, about one teaspoon. Solid ghee from the fridge also works.
black peppercorns, or dried green peas, or small beads
a ruler and a marker pen, or a pencil to make small scratch marks on paper tape beside the ladle
a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand
a plate, a cloth, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water and keeps the tumbler steady. The child does not touch the ladle while it is in the water. After the test, a grown-up lifts the ladle out with a cloth.

schedule.what: Put four butter dots along a ladle, guess the order, stand it in hot water and time each peppercorn as it falls.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the ladle with the four dots and write the time beside each one.

setup.art: A dry steel ladle lying on a plate, with a ruler beside it and small marks at 2, 4, 6 and 8 cm from the bowl's rim.
setup.caption: 1. Mark the handle at 2, 4, 6 and 8 cm above where the water will reach.

setup.art: Four small butter dots on the marks, each with a black peppercorn pressed into it.
setup.caption: 2. Put a small dot of cold butter on each mark and press a peppercorn into it.

setup.art: The ladle leaning in a steel tumbler of steaming water, dots on the upper side of the handle, a phone timer beside it.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up pours the hot water. Lean the ladle in and start the timer.

flow.do: 1. Stand the empty ladle in the empty tumbler, leaning on the rim. 2. Mark where the top of the water will be, about two-thirds up the tumbler. 3. Measure up the handle from that line and mark 2, 4, 6 and 8 cm.
flow.say: We are going to see how heat travels up a ladle. First we mark four places on the handle, each 2 cm further from the water.
flow.kid: Mark the handle at 2, 4, 6 and 8 cm. Measure from the water line.
flow.parent: Mark the steel with a marker, or stick a strip of paper beside the handle and mark that. Do not wrap tape round the handle at the dots, because tape slows the heat.

flow.do: 1. Take the ladle out. 2. Put a dot of cold butter, about half a pea, on each mark, on the top side of the handle. 3. Press a peppercorn into each dot. 4. Put one more dot and peppercorn on the spare spoon on the plate.
flow.say: Make every dot the same size. Why do you think that matters?
flow.kid: Make four small butter dots, all the same size. Press a peppercorn into each one.

ask.q: Why must the dots be the same size?
good: A big dot takes longer to melt, so it would not be fair.
So only the distance is different.

flow.parent: Work quickly, so the butter stays cold. In a hot room, do this test in the coolest part of the day. The spare dot on the plate shows whether the room alone melts the butter.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess the order the peppercorns will fall, and how long each will take. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: Which peppercorn will fall first? Which last? Will they fall close together, or with long gaps? Will the top one fall at all? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which peppercorn falls first. Will the top one fall? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that one will fall first?
good: It is nearest the hot water.
Heat goes up, so the top one.

flow.parent: Take any guess with a reason, and do not correct it. Some children say the top one, because 'heat rises'. The test will answer it.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pours hot water into the tumbler up to the water line. 2. Lean the ladle in with the dots facing up, and start the timer. 3. Watch closely. 4. Write the time each peppercorn falls.
flow.say: Watch the dots. Tell me the moment a peppercorn moves, and I will read the timer.
flow.kid: Do not touch the ladle. Watch the dots. Shout when a peppercorn falls.
flow.parent: With water just off the boil, the dot at 2 cm usually falls within about a minute, and the dot at 4 cm a few minutes later. The dot at 6 cm takes longer still, and the dot at 8 cm may never fall. The exact times depend on the ladle, the water and the room. Stop after 12 minutes. If the room dot on the plate also melts, the room is too warm: do it again later, with the dots a little bigger.
flow.think: Did the waits between the peppercorns stay the same, or grow longer?

flow.do: Before the water cools, hold your palm about one finger-width from the middle of the handle, without touching it.
flow.say: Hold your hand near the handle but do not touch it. Can you feel any warmth?
flow.kid: Hold your hand near the handle. Do not touch. Is it warm?
flow.parent: Your child may feel a faint warmth. The handle is giving some of its heat to the air. That is part of why the far dots get so little.

flow.do: Look at the times together.
flow.say: The bottom dot fell first. Then each dot took longer than the one before. Why do you think the waits grew longer?
flow.kid: Each dot took longer than the one before. Why?

check.q: On a steel ladle in hot water, which peppercorn falls first?
options: The one at the top, because heat rises
They all fall at the same time
check.why: The heat comes from the water, so it reaches the nearest part of the steel first. Picking 'the top' is a common guess, because hot air rises. But inside a solid, heat moves from hot to cool, whichever way that is. If you guessed 'all at once', look at your times: the heat needed time to travel.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three things: what I think, what I saw, and why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A strong answer sounds like this. What I think: heat travels up the steel slowly, near parts first. What I saw: the 2 cm peppercorn fell first, then the 4 cm one, and the 8 cm one never fell. Why: each part of the ladle has to warm up before it passes heat on, and some heat goes into the air.

experiments.title: Flat or Upright: does heat only go up?
experiments.context: In this experiment you test whether heat in a spoon goes only upwards. One spoon stands up in hot water and one lies flat.
experiments.question: Does heat move along a steel spoon as fast when the spoon lies flat as when it stands up?
experiments.predict: One spoon stands up in hot water. One lies flat, with its bowl in the water. Which butter dot will melt first? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two spoons of the same kind. Put one butter dot on each, 3 cm from the water, the same size. Use the same hot water for both, poured at the same time. Only the direction of the spoon changes.

materials.item: two steel spoons of the same kind and size
a steel tumbler, for the upright spoon
a wide, shallow steel bowl or a deep plate, for the flat spoon
two or three books, stacked to the height of the bowl's rim, to hold the flat spoon's handle level
hot water from a kettle or a pan, just off the boil, poured by a grown-up
butter straight from the fridge, about one teaspoon. Solid ghee from the fridge also works.
black peppercorns, or dried green peas, or small beads
a ruler, a timer, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water. Keep the bowl away from the table's edge. Do not touch the spoons while they are in the water.

schedule.what: Test one spoon upright and one lying flat, with a butter dot 3 cm from the water on each.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw both spoons with arrows showing which way the heat moved.

setup.art: Two steel spoons side by side, each with a butter dot and a peppercorn 3 cm from the bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Put a butter dot with a peppercorn 3 cm up each spoon.

setup.art: One spoon standing in a steel tumbler of hot water. Beside it, the other spoon lying level, its bowl in a shallow bowl of hot water and its handle resting on a stack of books.
setup.caption: 2. Stand one spoon up. Lay the other flat, its handle on books.

setup.art: A child watching both spoons with a timer, both peppercorns about to slide.
setup.caption: 3. Time when each peppercorn falls.

flow.do: 1. Stack books beside the shallow bowl, up to its rim. 2. Lay one spoon with its bowl in the empty bowl and its handle on the books. 3. Stand the other spoon in the tumbler. 4. Put a butter dot with a peppercorn 3 cm from where the water will reach, on each.
flow.say: One spoon stands up, and one lies flat. Both dots are the same distance from the water.
flow.kid: One spoon stands up. One lies flat. Put a dot on each, 3 cm up.
flow.parent: The flat spoon's handle should rest on the books, not on the steel rim of the bowl, because the hot rim would warm it from the side.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: Which peppercorn will fall first, the standing one or the flat one? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which falls first, standing or flat? Why?

good: The standing one, because heat goes up.
The same, because heat goes from hot to cool.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pours hot water into the tumbler and the bowl at the same time, to the same depth on each spoon. 2. Start the timer. 3. Write down when each peppercorn falls.
flow.say: Watch both dots. Tell me when each peppercorn falls.
flow.kid: Do not touch the spoons. Watch both dots. Call out when one falls.
flow.parent: Both peppercorns usually fall within a minute or so of each other. A small difference can come from the water depth or from the shallow water cooling faster. If the flat one is a little slower, ask your child whether the water in the bowl stayed as hot.

flow.do: Compare the times and talk about them.
flow.say: The flat spoon got hot along its handle too. So does heat in a spoon only go up?
flow.kid: The flat spoon warmed too. Does heat only go up?

check.q: A steel spoon lies flat with its bowl in hot water. What happens to its handle?
options: It stays cold, because heat only goes up
It warms, because heat moves from the hot end to the cool end
It warms only if the spoon is tilted up
check.why: Inside a solid, heat moves from hot to cool in any direction: up, down or sideways. Hot air and hot water rise, which is where 'heat rises' comes from. But the steel of a spoon does not move, so the heat just spreads towards the cooler parts.

activities.title: The Spoon in the Tea: where does the warmth come from?
activities.context: This short activity starts the unit. A steel spoon stands in a hot drink, and your child feels its handle slowly warm.

materials.item: a cup or tumbler of hot tea, coffee or milk, made by a grown-up
two steel spoons of the same kind

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the hot drink and touches the spoon handle first, to check it is only warm.

schedule.what: Stand a steel spoon in a hot drink, feel its handle after two minutes, and compare it with a spoon on the table.

activities.record: Draw the cup and the spoon. Colour the parts of the spoon you think are warm.

setup.art: A steaming cup of tea with a steel spoon standing in it, and a second steel spoon lying on the table beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Stand one spoon in the hot drink. Leave the other on the table.

setup.art: A child touching the tip of each spoon handle with one finger, one hand on each.
setup.caption: 2. After two minutes, touch the top of each handle.

flow.do: 1. Stand one steel spoon in the hot drink. 2. Put the other spoon on the table. 3. Wait two minutes.
flow.say: One spoon goes in the tea. The other stays on the table. In two minutes, will their handles feel the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One spoon goes in the tea. One stays out. Will the handles feel the same?

flow.do: 1. Touch the top of the spoon handle yourself first. 2. If it is only warm, let your child touch the top of both handles.
flow.say: Touch the top of each handle. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Touch the top of each handle. Which one is warm?
flow.parent: The handle of the spoon in the tea should feel warm, and the other should not. If the tea is very hot, the handle can get too hot to hold. Check first.

ask.q: The top of the handle never touched the tea. How did it get warm?
good: The heat went up the spoon.
The tea warmed the bottom, and the bottom warmed the top.

flow.do: Write down your child's idea about how the handle got warm. Do not explain yet.
flow.say: That is a good question to keep. We will test it with a ladle and some butter.
flow.kid: How did the heat get up the spoon? Keep your idea. We will test it.
flow.parent: Keep the explanation for after the Ladle Line test. Your child's own idea now makes the test more interesting.

activities.title: Who Melts the Ice? Your hand or the plate
activities.context: In this activity your child holds an ice cube in their fist while another sits on a plate. It shows that heat moves from the hand into the ice.

materials.item: two ice cubes of the same size
a plate and a small bowl
a timer and a towel

activities.safety: Hold the ice for 3 minutes at most, and swap hands if it hurts. Dry your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: Hold one ice cube in a fist over a bowl and leave one on a plate for 3 minutes. Compare what is left.

activities.record: Draw the two ice cubes after 3 minutes. Draw an arrow to show which way the heat moved.

setup.art: Two ice cubes of the same size, one on a plate and one in a child's open palm above a small bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Put one ice cube on a plate. Hold the other in your fist over a bowl.

setup.art: After 3 minutes: a large ice cube on the plate, and a much smaller one in the child's palm with water in the bowl below.
setup.caption: 2. After 3 minutes, compare the two cubes.

flow.do: 1. Put one ice cube on the plate. 2. Your child holds the other in a closed fist over the bowl. 3. Start a 3-minute timer.
flow.say: Which ice cube will melt faster, the one in your hand or the one on the plate? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Hold one ice cube in your fist. Which will melt faster? Why?

flow.do: When the timer ends, open the fist and put the cube on the plate next to the other.
flow.say: Look at both cubes. Which one is smaller? And how does your hand feel?
flow.kid: Open your hand. Which cube is smaller? How does your hand feel?
flow.parent: The cube from the fist is usually much smaller, with water in the bowl. Your hand is about 30 to 35 °C on the outside, warmer than the room air in most homes, and it touches the ice all over.

flow.do: Talk about which way the heat went.
flow.say: Your hand feels cold. Did cold go into your hand, or did heat go out of it?
flow.kid: Did cold go into your hand? Or did heat go out?

check.q: Why did the ice in your fist melt faster?
options: Cold moved from the ice into your hand
Heat moved from your warm hand into the ice
check.why: Heat moves from a warmer thing to a cooler one. Your hand was warmer than the ice, so heat moved into the ice and melted it. Your hand felt cold because it lost heat. Cold is not a thing that moves. Squeezing can break ice, but it does not melt much of it.

activities.title: Draw the Heat Inside the Ladle
activities.context: In this activity your child draws what they think is happening inside the steel of the ladle, where nobody can see.

materials.item: paper, a pencil and red, orange and yellow colour pencils

schedule.what: Draw a zoomed-in picture of the ladle handle, showing how the heat travels.

activities.record: Keep the drawing in your science notebook.

setup.art: A drawing of a ladle in hot water, with a big magnifying circle over the handle.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the ladle, with a big circle to zoom into the handle.

setup.art: Inside the circle, rows of small balls: red and shaking near the water, orange in the middle, yellow and still near the top.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the tiny particles inside. Show how they shake.

flow.do: Ask your child to draw the ladle in hot water, with a big zoom-in circle over the handle.
flow.say: Imagine you could zoom in on the steel, far closer than any magnifying glass. What would you see?
flow.kid: Draw the ladle. Draw a big circle to zoom in on the handle.

flow.do: Tell them the steel is made of tiny particles that shake more when they are hotter. Ask them to draw the particles near the water and near the top.
flow.say: Steel is made of tiny particles. Hotter particles shake faster. Draw how they shake near the water, and near the top.
flow.kid: Draw tiny balls in the circle. Hot ones shake a lot. Cool ones shake a little.
flow.parent: A strong drawing shows the particles staying in their places, with bigger shake lines near the hot end, and smaller ones further up. Some children draw heat as a liquid running up. Ask: 'Did anything flow up the ladle?'

flow.do: Ask your child to explain their drawing.
flow.say: Tell me about your drawing. How does the shaking get from the bottom to the top?
flow.kid: Explain your drawing. How does the shaking get to the top?

ask.q: How does the shaking get to the top?
good: Each particle bumps the next one.
It is passed on, one by one.

challenges.title: A Cool Grip for a Hot Ladle
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You make a grip for a steel ladle that keeps your hand cool, and test it with butter.
challenges.problem: A steel ladle in hot sambar gets hot along its handle. Make a grip for the handle, from things at home, so that the outside of the grip stays cool.
constraints: The grip must come off again, so the ladle can be washed.
You test it the same way as the Ladle Line: a butter dot with a peppercorn on the outside of the grip, 4 cm above the water.
materials: a folded cotton cloth, a woollen sock, newspaper, rubber bands, a wooden clothes peg, cardboard or a cork
butter from the fridge and peppercorns
a steel tumbler of hot water, poured by a grown-up
general: Wrap the handle in several layers of cloth or newspaper, held with rubber bands. The cloth and the air caught in it are insulators.
Slide a thick cork or a wooden peg onto the handle, like the wooden handles on a tawa.
creative: Wrap the handle loosely, so a layer of air is caught between the steel and the cloth.
Use a strip of cardboard folded into a tube that does not touch the steel all the way round.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own grip. Draw it, make it, and test it against a bare ladle. Which material worked best, and why?

setup.art: A steel ladle with a grip of folded cloth held on by two rubber bands, and a butter dot with a peppercorn on the outside of the cloth.
setup.caption: 1. Make a grip and put a butter dot on the outside of it.

setup.art: Two ladles side by side in tumblers of hot water: one bare with a butter dot on the steel, one with the cloth grip and a dot on the cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Test it next to a bare ladle.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Look at the materials and draw two ideas for a grip.
flow.say: Which of these things let heat through slowly? How could we use them on the handle?
flow.kid: Which things let heat through slowly? Draw two ideas for a grip.

flow.do: Make the grip. Put it on the handle so its bottom edge is about 2 cm above the water line.
flow.say: Make your grip. Leave a little bare steel between the water and the grip.
flow.kid: Make your grip. Put it on the handle, above the water.

flow.do: 1. Put a butter dot with a peppercorn on the outside of the grip, 4 cm above the water. 2. Put one on a bare ladle at 4 cm too. 3. A grown-up pours hot water into two tumblers. 4. Stand both ladles in and time them.
flow.say: Which peppercorn will fall first? Why do you think so? Let's watch.
flow.kid: Do not touch the ladles. Watch both dots. Which falls first?
flow.parent: The dot on the bare steel should fall within a few minutes. The dot on a thick cloth or cork grip usually stays put for the whole 12 minutes. The steel under the grip still gets warm, but the heat moves through the cloth very slowly.

flow.do: Read the usual and the creative ideas. Then talk about your own.
flow.say: Your grip slowed the heat. What could make it even better?
flow.kid: Your grip slowed the heat. How could you make it better?

challenges.title: Soften the Butter Fast, with No Flame
challenges.context: This is a problem-solving challenge. You use what you know about conductors to soften cold butter quickly, using only hot water.
challenges.problem: Ammamma needs soft butter for her biscuits, but the butter is hard from the fridge. You have a bowl of hot water but no flame. Find the quickest way to soften a cube of butter.
constraints: The butter must not touch the water.
No flame, no stove and no microwave.
Each cube of butter is the same size, about 1 cm on each side.
materials: three small cubes of cold butter
a small steel katori, a plastic box lid, and a paper cup
a big bowl of hot water, poured by a grown-up
general: Put each cube in a different small container and float or stand the containers in the hot water. The steel katori usually softens its butter first, because steel is a better conductor of heat than plastic or paper.
creative: Cut the butter into small pieces first, so more of it touches the warm steel.
Press the butter flat against the bottom of the katori.
challenges.your_turn: Now try your own idea. Which way softened the butter fastest? What did the winning way have that the others did not?

setup.art: A big bowl of steaming water with a steel katori, a plastic lid and a paper cup floating in it, each holding a small butter cube.
setup.caption: 1. Put one butter cube in each container, in the hot water.

setup.art: The butter in the steel katori melted to a soft puddle, while the cube in the paper cup still has sharp corners.
setup.caption: 2. Check every minute. Which one is soft first?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child which container will soften the butter first, and why.
flow.say: Which container will let the heat reach the butter fastest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which container will soften the butter first? Why?

flow.do: 1. A grown-up pours hot water into the big bowl. 2. Put the three containers in, each with a butter cube. 3. Press each cube gently with a spoon every minute.
flow.say: Check each cube every minute. Which one goes soft first?
flow.kid: Press each cube gently with a spoon. Which is soft first?
flow.parent: The butter in the steel katori usually softens within a few minutes, and the paper cup is slowest. A light plastic lid may tip in the water, so hold it steady with a spoon.

flow.do: Talk about why the winner won. Then read the creative ideas and try one.
flow.say: Why did the steel katori work best?
flow.kid: Why did the steel one win?

quiz.p: A cup of hot tea stands in a room. Which way does heat move?
opts: From the room into the tea
From the tea into the room
It does not move
quiz.why: Heat moves from the hotter tea into the cooler room, until the tea is as warm as the room.

quiz.p: A steel spoon stands in hot milk. How does its handle get warm?
opts: Hot milk climbs up inside the spoon
Heat is passed up the steel, from part to part
The air pushes cold out of the spoon
quiz.why: This is conduction. Each part of the steel warms the part next to it. No milk climbs up.

quiz.p: Meena puts butter dots on a steel ladle at 2 cm and 6 cm above hot water. What will most likely happen?
opts: The 6 cm dot melts first
The 2 cm dot melts first, and the 6 cm dot much later or not at all
Both melt at the same moment
quiz.why: Heat reaches the nearest part first. The far part waits much longer, and gets less heat, because some leaks into the air.

quiz.p: Which of these is a good conductor of heat?
opts: A wooden spatula
An aluminium kadai
A plastic plate
quiz.why: Aluminium is a metal, and metals are good conductors of heat. Wood and plastic are insulators.

quiz.p: Why do pressure cookers have plastic handles?
opts: Plastic is cheaper than metal
Plastic is an insulator, so the handle stays cool enough to hold
Plastic makes the food cook faster
quiz.why: Heat moves through plastic very slowly, so the handle does not get hot quickly.

quiz.p: Priya holds an ice cube and her hand gets cold. Why?
opts: Cold moves from the ice into her hand
Heat moves from her hand into the ice
The ice is wet
quiz.why: Heat moves from warmer to cooler. Her hand loses heat to the ice, so it feels cold, and the ice melts.

quiz.p: Farhan wants to test how far heat travels up a ladle. Which test is fair?
opts: Dots of different sizes at different heights
Dots of the same size at different heights
One dot, moved about during the test
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here it is the height, so every dot must be the same size.

quiz.p: A steel spoon lies flat, with only its bowl in hot water. What happens to its handle?
opts: It warms up, because heat moves from hot to cool in any direction
It stays cold, because heat only goes up
It gets colder
quiz.why: Inside a solid, heat goes from hot to cool, up, down or sideways.

quiz.p: Why do the particles in a hot spoon pass heat along?
opts: They flow up the handle like water
They shake faster and bump the particles next to them
They get bigger
quiz.why: Hot particles shake faster. They bump their neighbours, which then shake faster too. The particles stay in place.

opts: Copper
Stainless steel
Lead
quiz.why: Copper is one of the best conductors of heat. Stainless steel and lead are much slower.

quiz.p: Kavya's ladle dots fell at 1 minute, 3 minutes and 8 minutes. What does this tell her?
opts: Heat moved at one steady speed
Heat took longer and longer to reach parts further from the water
The water was getting hotter
quiz.why: The waits grew from 2 minutes to 5 minutes. Heat gets slower as it travels further along the steel.

quiz.p: Which of these is mostly conduction?
opts: The Sun warming your face
A hot tawa cooking a dosa
Steam rising from a pot
quiz.why: The dosa touches the hot tawa, so heat passes straight into it. The Sun is radiation, and rising steam is convection.

worksheets.title: Which Way Is the Heat Going? (core)

items.p: Which way does heat move by itself?
opts: From a cooler thing to a hotter thing
From a hotter thing to a cooler thing
Only upwards
items.why: Heat moves by itself from hotter to cooler, until both are equally warm. 'Only upwards' is a common mix-up with hot air rising.

items.p: Heat moving through a solid, from each tiny part to the part next to it, is called ____.
items.why: Conduction is how heat travels through a solid like a steel spoon.

items.p: When you hold an ice cube, cold moves from the ice into your hand.
items.why: False. Heat moves from your warm hand into the ice. Your hand feels cold because it is losing heat. Cold does not move.

items.p: Sort these into good conductors of heat and insulators of heat.
items.a: see items
items.why: The metals are good conductors of heat. Wood, plastic, cloth and paper are insulators. A strong sorter asks 'Is it a metal?'

items.p: Kavya put butter dots on a steel ladle at 2, 4, 6 and 8 cm above hot water. Put the dots in the order their peppercorns fell, first to last.
items.why: Heat reaches the parts nearest the hot water first, then moves further along. So the nearest dot falls first.

items.p: In the Ladle Line test, the peppercorn at 8 cm often never falls. Give two reasons why.
items.a: The heat has a long way to go, and each part of the steel must warm up before it passes heat on. Also, the handle gives some of its heat to the air all along the way, so little is left by 8 cm.
items.why: A strong answer gives both reasons: the slow part-by-part travel, and heat leaking into the air.

items.p: Draw a tumbler of hot milk with a steel spoon standing in it. Draw red arrows to show where the heat moves.
items.a: Arrows from the milk into the spoon, up the spoon handle, and from the handle and the tumbler out into the air.
items.why: A strong drawing shows heat going from the hot milk to cooler things: up the spoon, and out into the air.
items.art: An empty box with a faint outline of a tumbler.

items.p: Lakshmi pours hot rasam into a cold steel bowl. What happens to the bowl?
opts: It stays cold, because steel is cold
It warms up, because heat moves from the rasam into the steel
It makes the rasam colder than the room
items.why: Heat moves from the hot rasam into the cooler steel, so the bowl warms. It can cool the rasam a little, but never below the room's temperature.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: energy moving from hotter to cooler
heat passed through a solid, part by part
a material heat moves through quickly
a material heat moves through slowly
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four words come up all through the unit.

items.p: A wooden spoon left in hot payasam gets a hot handle just as fast as a steel spoon.
items.why: False. Wood is an insulator of heat, so heat moves up a wooden spoon very slowly. Its handle stays cool for a long time.

items.p: Why does a dosa tawa have a metal plate but a wooden handle?
items.a: The metal plate is a good conductor, so heat from the flame moves quickly into the dosa. The wooden handle is an insulator, so the heat reaches the cook's hand only very slowly.
items.why: A strong answer explains both parts: where the cook wants heat to go, and where not.

items.p: Divya tests a ladle. She puts a big butter dot at 2 cm and a tiny butter dot at 6 cm. Why is this not a fair test?
opts: The dots are different sizes, so size changes how fast they melt
The ladle is steel
She used butter, not ghee
items.why: A big dot takes longer to melt than a tiny one. In a fair test only the distance should change, so every dot must be the same size.

items.p: Label this picture of a spoon in hot tea: the hot end, the cool end, and the way the heat moves.
items.a: The hot end is the part in the tea. The cool end is the top of the handle. An arrow goes from the hot end up to the cool end.
items.why: Heat moves from the hot end towards the cool end.
items.art: A spoon standing in a cup of tea, with three blank label lines: one to the bowl in the tea, one to the top of the handle, and one beside the handle for an arrow.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? Steel, copper, wood, aluminium.
items.a: Wood
items.why: Wood is an insulator of heat. Steel, copper and aluminium are metals, which are good conductors.

items.p: Think about your own Ladle Line test. Write what you think, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
items.a: What I think: heat travels up the steel slowly, nearest parts first. What I saw: the 2 cm peppercorn fell first, and each one after took longer. Why: each part has to warm before it can pass heat to the next.
items.why: A strong answer uses the child's own times as evidence.

items.p: Kavya and Meena are arguing about a steel spoon lying flat, with only its bowl in hot water.

views.says: The handle will stay cold, because heat rises, and this handle is not higher than the water.
The handle will get warm, because heat goes from hot to cool, whichever way that is.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use the Flat or Upright test as evidence. Then say what Kavya has partly right.
items.a: Meena is right for a solid spoon: in the test, the flat spoon's peppercorn fell at about the same time as the upright one. Kavya has partly right that hot air and hot water rise.
items.why: A strong answer uses the test's result, and gives Kavya fair credit for what is true about hot air.

items.p: Farhan stands a steel spoon and an aluminium spoon of the same size in the same hot water. Each has a butter dot 4 cm up. Which peppercorn will most likely fall first?
opts: The steel one
The aluminium one
They will fall together
items.why: Aluminium carries heat many times faster than stainless steel. Both are metals, but metals are not all alike.

items.p: A pressure cooker has an aluminium or steel body and plastic handles. Why is each part made of that material?
items.a: The metal body is a good conductor, so heat from the flame gets into the food quickly. The plastic handles are insulators, so the heat reaches your hand very slowly.
items.why: A strong answer links each material to where the heat should go.

items.p: Three rods of the same length stand in hot water: copper, steel and wood. Put them in order, from the one whose top gets warm first to the one that gets warm last.
items.why: Copper is one of the best conductors of heat. Steel is a metal too, but slower. Wood is an insulator.

items.p: Inside a solid, heat can only move upwards.
items.why: False. Inside a solid, heat moves from hot to cool in any direction. Hot air and hot water rise, but a solid does not flow.

items.p: Nila wraps cloth round the middle of a ladle handle and stands the ladle in hot water. Does the steel under the cloth still get warm? Explain.
items.a: Yes. Heat still travels up the steel inside the cloth. But the cloth is an insulator, so heat goes through it to the outside very slowly, and the outside of the cloth stays cool.
items.why: A strong answer says the steel still conducts, and the cloth only slows heat getting out to the hand.

items.p: Revathi holds an ice cube in a thick woollen glove. Will it melt faster or slower than in her bare hand? Why?
items.a: Slower. The wool and the air caught in it are insulators, so heat from her hand reaches the ice more slowly.
items.why: A strong answer says which way the heat moves (hand to ice) and why the glove slows it.

items.p: The best conductors of heat, like silver and copper, are also the best conductors of ____.
items.why: In metals, free electrons carry both heat and electricity.

items.p: Draw a zoomed-in picture of the steel inside a ladle handle, with the hot end on the left and the cool end on the right. Show how the tiny particles move.
items.a: Rows of particles staying in place. Those on the left shake hard, and the shaking gets smaller towards the right.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the particles staying in their places and passing the shaking along, not flowing.
items.art: A long empty rectangle with 'hot' written at the left end and 'cool' at the right end.

items.p: Sort these parts of kitchen things. Should each part be a good conductor of heat or an insulator?
items: the knob on a kettle lid
the bottom of a cooking pot
items.a: see items
items.why: The parts that should pass heat to the food are good conductors. The parts you touch are insulators.

items.p: On the Ladle Line, the wait between the 2 cm and 4 cm dots was short. The wait between the 4 cm and 6 cm dots was longer. Why?
opts: The butter higher up was bigger
Each part of the steel must warm up before it passes heat on, and some heat leaks into the air
The water got hotter
items.why: Heat is passed on part by part, and loses some to the air on the way. So it takes longer and longer to reach parts further away. The water was cooling, not getting hotter.

items.p: Match each example to the way the heat moves.
pairs: A steel spoon in tea gets a warm handle
Hot water rises from the bottom of a pan
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Conduction is through a solid. Convection is a moving liquid or gas carrying heat. Radiation is heat travelling as rays, even across empty space.

items.p: Label the part of this pan that should be a good conductor of heat, and the part that should be an insulator.
items.a: The metal pan is the conductor. The handle is the insulator.
items.why: The pan passes heat to the food. The handle keeps it from the hand.
items.art: A frying pan with a long handle, and two blank label lines.

items.p: Copper carries heat faster than stainless steel.
items.why: True. Copper carries heat about 25 times faster than stainless steel. That is why some steel vessels have a copper bottom.

items.p: Arjun says, 'If the ladle were twice as long, its top end would get even hotter.' Is he right? Explain.
items.a: No. The top end would be further from the hot water. The heat would take longer to get there, and more would leak into the air on the way. So the top would stay cooler.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the Ladle Line showed: further parts get heat later and less of it.

items.p: No tiny particle of the spoon travelled up to the handle. So what did move up the spoon? Explain in your own words.
items.a: The shaking moved up. Particles at the hot end shook faster and bumped their neighbours, which shook faster and bumped the next ones. The energy was passed along, while every particle stayed in its place.
items.why: A strong answer separates the particles, which stay put, from the energy, which is passed on.

items.p: A family is buying a new cooking vessel.

views.says: Buy the steel vessel with a copper bottom. Heat spreads across it fast, so the food does not burn in one spot.
Buy the plain steel one. It costs less and is easier to keep clean.
Buy the plain steel one, but cook on a lower flame and stir more.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses a fact: copper is a much better conductor than steel, so it spreads heat evenly. It also admits a fair point, such as cost or cleaning, from another side.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Each choice has a real trade-off.

items.p: Why do some steel vessels have a layer of copper or aluminium on the bottom?
opts: To make them heavier
Copper and aluminium spread heat across the bottom faster than steel
To keep the food cold
items.why: Copper and aluminium are much better conductors than stainless steel. So the heat spreads across the whole bottom, and food is less likely to burn in one spot.

items.p: A blanket keeps you warm on a cold night. Does the blanket make heat? Explain where the warmth comes from.
items.a: No. The blanket makes no heat. Your body makes heat from food. The blanket and the air in it are insulators, so they slow your heat leaving into the cold room.
items.why: A strong answer says the heat comes from the body, and the blanket only slows it escaping.

items.p: Design a cup that keeps tea hot for a long time and is cool to hold. Draw it and label what each part is made of.
items.a: For example, a cup with two walls and air between them, a lid, and a wooden or plastic handle.
items.why: A strong design uses insulators, such as air, plastic or wood, where heat should not escape or reach the hand.
items.art: An empty box for a drawing.

items.p: A steel tumbler and a wooden board that have sat in the same room all day are at the same temperature, even though the steel feels colder.
items.why: True. Things left together reach the same temperature. The steel feels colder because it carries heat out of your hand faster.

items.p: Here are made-up Ladle Line results: 2 cm fell at 1 minute, 4 cm at 3 minutes, 6 cm at 8 minutes, and 8 cm never fell. What do they show?
opts: Heat moves at one steady speed
Heat takes longer and longer to reach parts further away
The butter was different at each dot
items.why: The waits were 2 minutes, then 5 minutes, then more than the rest of the test. Heat is passed on part by part and leaks away, so it gets slower the further it goes.

items.p: Arjun says, 'The 8 cm peppercorn never fell, so no heat got past 6 cm.' Find the mistake in his thinking.
items.a: Some heat did get past 6 cm, but not enough to melt the butter. The steel at 8 cm was a little warmer than before, just not warm enough.
items.why: A strong answer sees that 'not enough to melt butter' is not the same as 'no heat at all'.

items.p: In a metal, tiny particles called ____ move freely between the atoms and carry heat quickly.
items.why: Free electrons are why metals carry heat and electricity so well.

items.p: Sort these by how the heat moves.
items: a hot tawa warming a dosa
your hand warming a cold tumbler
warm air rising above an iron box
feeling the warmth of a fire from across a room
items.a: see items
items.why: Conduction is through touching solids. Convection is a liquid or gas rising and sinking. Radiation is heat travelling as rays.

items.p: Which is the odd one out, and why? A wooden tawa handle, a cloth pot holder, a coconut-shell ladle, a steel serving spoon.
items.a: The steel serving spoon
items.why: The other three are insulators that keep heat away from a hand. The steel spoon is a good conductor.

items.p: Label this zoomed-in picture of a metal: an atom, a free electron, the hot end and the cool end.
items.a: The big balls in rows are atoms. The small dots moving between them are free electrons. The hot end is where they move fastest.
items.why: Free electrons carry energy from the hot end to the cool end.
items.art: Big balls in neat rows with small dots between them, and four blank label lines.

items.p: A garden lizard lies flat on a sunny wall in the morning. What problem does the lizard have, and how does lying flat help?
items.a: The lizard's body is cold after the night, so their muscles work slowly. Lying flat on a warm wall lets heat move from the wall into their belly by conduction, and the sun warms their back too. Then they can run and hunt.
items.why: A strong answer names the lizard's problem first, then how the heat moves from the wall to them.

items.p: A fridge moves heat from its cold inside to the warmer kitchen without using any electricity.
items.why: False. Heat never moves by itself from cooler to hotter. A fridge needs electricity to pump heat out of its inside.

items.p: Your body is warmer than the room, so heat is leaving you all day. Why doesn't your body cool down to the temperature of the room?
items.a: Your body keeps making heat from the food you eat, so it replaces the heat it loses.
items.why: A strong answer says heat is lost all the time and food energy replaces it.

open_questions.q: What is the best possible conductor of heat?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists keep finding materials that carry heat better, such as diamond and very thin sheets of carbon called graphene. Nobody knows the limit.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does heat move through glass, wood and other materials whose particles are not in neat rows?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand heat moving through neat crystals well. In jumbled materials it is harder to work out, and they are still studying it.

open_questions.q: Will everything in the universe one day be the same temperature?
open_questions.why_open: Heat keeps spreading from hot places to cool ones. Some scientists think the universe will slowly even out, but nobody knows for sure.

maths.context: This is about the Ladle Line, where you time butter dots melting along a ladle in hot water. These are made-up results.
maths.problem: Meenakshi's peppercorns fell at 40 seconds, 150 seconds and 360 seconds. How long was the wait between the first and the second? And between the second and the third?
maths.explain: 150 minus 40 is 110. 360 minus 150 is 210. The second wait was almost twice as long as the first. So the heat took longer and longer to reach each dot.
maths.why_maths: Taking each time from the next one shows how long each wait was, and that the waits grow.

maths.context: This is about the Ladle Line test, where butter dots go along a ladle handle.
maths.problem: Kavya's ladle handle is 20 cm long. She wants a butter dot every 4 cm, starting 4 cm from the water. How many dots can she fit?
maths.explain: The dots go at 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 cm. 20 divided by 4 is 5. So she can fit 5 dots.
maths.why_maths: Dividing tells you how many equal steps fit along the handle before you start.

maths.context: This is about the Flat or Upright test, where one spoon stands up and one lies flat in hot water. These are made-up results.
maths.problem: The upright spoon's peppercorn fell at 95 seconds. The flat spoon's fell at 105 seconds. What is the difference? Is that enough to say heat goes up faster?
maths.answer: 10 seconds. That is too small to be sure.
maths.explain: 105 minus 95 is 10. A difference of 10 seconds can come from a slightly bigger dot or shallower water. To be sure, you would do the test again. If the flat one were not always slower, the difference was luck.
maths.why_maths: Working out the difference, then asking if it is big enough, stops us from reading too much into a small number.

maths.context: This is about the Ladle Line. Here are made-up waits between peppercorns.
maths.problem: Divya's waits between peppercorns were 1 minute, then 2 minutes, then 4 minutes. If the pattern carried on, how long would the next wait be?
maths.explain: Each wait is double the one before: 1, 2, 4. Double 4 is 8. In a real test the pattern is not exact, and the far dot may never fall at all, because heat leaks into the air.
maths.why_maths: Spotting a pattern lets you predict the next result, then check it against what really happens.

maths.context: This is about the butter softening challenge, where cubes of butter sit in different containers in hot water. These are made-up results.
maths.problem: The butter in the steel katori went soft in 3 minutes. The butter in the plastic lid took 7 minutes, and in the paper cup 11 minutes. How much longer did the paper cup take than the steel katori?
maths.explain: 11 minus 3 is 8. The steel katori is a good conductor, so heat reached the butter fastest.
maths.why_maths: Taking one time from another shows how big the difference between materials really is.

roots.context: We have watched heat travel up a ladle, part by part. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: On your ladle, the peppercorn nearest the water fell first, and each one after took longer. Heat must warm each part of the steel before it can move on to the next. Along the way, some of it leaks into the air. So heat slows down as it travels along a handle, and the far end may stay cool.
deep_truth.habit: We picture heat running through a spoon like water through a pipe, at one steady speed. But heat in a solid is handed on part by part, so it gets slower the further it goes, and some escapes on the way.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Ladle Line, the waits between the falling peppercorns grew longer, and the 8 cm dot often never fell. A palm held near the handle felt warmth leaving it into the air.

three.who_am_i: Your body is warmer than most things around you, so your heat is moving into the air, the floor and your clothes all day.
three.what_is_life: A garden lizard is cold and slow after the night. Lying flat on a sun-warmed wall, they take in its heat through their belly, and soon they can run.
three.what_is_this_world: The inside of the Earth is very hot. Its heat is creeping out through solid rock towards the surface all the time.

roots.thread: A steel ladle looks like one solid thing. Heat shows that it is also a huge number of tiny parts, each touching the next. The hot water warms the first part, that part warms the next, and so on along the handle. How warm each part gets depends on its neighbours. One ladle, made of many parts, with one heat passing through them all.

teachings.teaching: Cold things grow warm, the warm grows cold, the wet dries and the dry grows wet.
teachings.link: In your tests, the hot water cooled while the ladle warmed, and your warm hand cooled while the ice melted. Heat keeps moving from warm to cool, so warm and cold things keep changing into each other.

teachings.source: Samyutta Nikaya 12.21 (the Buddha's teaching of dependent arising)
teachings.teaching: When this is, that is. When this arises, that arises. When this is not, that is not.
teachings.link: Each part of the ladle grew warm only because the part before it was warm. When the water was taken away, the warmth along the handle faded too.

science.text: Heat moves by itself only from hotter to cooler things. Scientists call this the second law of thermodynamics.
In metals, free electrons carry most of the heat. That is why good conductors of electricity are also good conductors of heat.

other_view.view: Heat moving along a ladle is just particles and electrons bumping into each other. Saying that each part 'depends on' its neighbour is a nice way to put it, but it adds nothing to the physics.

playtest: The Ladle Line was thought through for a stainless steel ladle in water just off the boil, in a room of 25 to 32 °C. Stainless steel is a slow metal, so the 2 cm and 4 cm dots melt within minutes, the 6 cm dot later, and the 8 cm dot often never. That missing fall is part of the result, not a failure. Butter from the fridge works best. In a very hot room, the spare dot on a spoon out of the water shows whether the room alone melts the butter, and the step says to wait for a cooler hour. Tape is not wrapped round the handle, because it would slow the heat. In Flat or Upright, the flat spoon's handle rests on books, not on a hot steel rim. No thermometer or bought item is needed for any part. The spine is the spoon in tea, the Ladle Line, the explanation cards, the ice in the fist, roots and the quiz, about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that heat moves through some metals faster than others? This card tells how.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1700s, people knew that metals carry heat quickly. A metal pot handle gets hot, and a wooden one does not. It was easy to guess that all metals, being hard and shiny, carry heat equally well. Benjamin Franklin, an American scientist and writer, thought of a simple way to test this. Coat wires of different metals with wax. Heat one end of each wire. Then see how far along each wire the wax melts. In 1780, Franklin gave the idea, and wires he had collected, to his friend Jan Ingenhousz. Ingenhousz was a Dutch doctor and scientist working in Vienna. He dipped each wire in melted wax, then put one end of each into hot oil. The wax melted along every wire, but much farther on some than on others. Silver carried heat best. Then came copper and gold, then tin, then iron and steel. Lead was slowest of all. So metals are not all alike. Your Ladle Line test works the same way, with butter in place of wax. Steel came low on Ingenhousz's list.
how_we_found_out.who: Benjamin Franklin, an American scientist, who suggested the test, and Jan Ingenhousz, a Dutch doctor and scientist, who did it
how_we_found_out.when: 1780 (Ingenhousz's letter to Franklin from Vienna, 5 December 1780, gives the results)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: It was easy to guess that all metals, being hard and shiny, carry heat equally well. The wax-coated wires showed that heat moves much faster through silver and copper than through iron, steel or lead.
